title: Peaks of the Balkans Trek: Full Guide
excerpt: The Peaks of the Balkans trek crosses Albania, Kosovo and Montenegro on foot. The full guide: the route day by day, border permits, guesthouses, season and cost.
seoTitle: Peaks of the Balkans Trek: Route, Border Permits and Cost

content.value: On the sixth day of the trek, on a summit at 2,366 m, three borders meet: those of Albania, Kosovo and Montenegro. A small monument marks the spot, and many trekkers stop there to stand in three countries at once. The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a walking journey through the Prokletije mountains, the Albanian Alps, that crosses the borders between the three countries on foot and stays in guesthouses run by local families in the mountain villages. With us it lasts 10 days, 8 of them walking days, and it is graded moderate: there is no technical climbing, but it takes good fitness for walking days of 13 to 22 km. The season runs from June to October.

There are quite a few questions worth answering before you decide: how do you cross a border in the middle of the mountains, what do you need to enter the three countries, where do you sleep and what do you eat, how hard is each day and what does the price include. This guide answers them, and it is based on the trek we run, from landing in Tirana to the flight home. If you are looking for a week in the mountains, without extreme altitude and with scenery few people know, this is a good place to start.

content.value: What the Peaks of the Balkans trek actually is

The Peaks of the Balkans is a waymarked walking trail in the Prokletije mountains, a jagged rock range that stretches between northern Albania, western Kosovo and eastern Montenegro. The local name of the mountains translates as the Accursed Mountains, and they are also known as the Albanian Alps. The full trail is a loop through the three countries, between shepherd villages, mountain lakes, forests and high passes. Some of the villages along the way can only be reached on foot or by mule track, and some are inhabited only in summer, when the shepherds come up with their flocks.

Part of this area was once a closed border zone, forbidden to enter. Along the trail you can still see the remains: an old military border post, Communist-era bunkers and pyramid-shaped border markers. What was once a dividing line has become a trail that connects three countries, and each of them has kept its own villages, cooking and customs of hospitality.

Our trek starts and ends in Shkodra, one of the oldest cities in Albania. You reach the starting point by boat across Lake Komani, and from there the walk goes through the Valbona valley, crosses into Montenegro and back, continues to Dobërdol, climbs Gjeravica peak in Kosovo, passes over the Triple Border Peak into Montenegro, and returns to Albania at the village of Theth for the last night in the mountains.
Our route, day by day
This is how the HighAir Peaks of the Balkans trek is built. The altitudes in brackets are those of the overnight stop or of the high point of that day:

items: Day 1: landing in Tirana and a drive of about two hours to Shkodra, an evening walk along the main street of the city and an opening dinner to meet the team and the group.

Day 2: drive to Lake Komani and a ferry ride between gorges and cliffs, a traditional lunch in a local town, and from the village of Dragobia a walk along the Valbona river to the village of Valbona (927 m). 7 km, 3 to 4 hours.

Day 3: a climb in steep switchbacks to the Prosllopi Pass (about 2,030 m), crossing the border into Montenegro, lunch in the Buri meadow and a gradual descent through forest to Çerem (1,150 m). 13 to 14 km, 7 to 8 hours.

Day 4: a gradual climb to the Montenegro border, through the shepherd hamlet of Balqin and the Gashi valley, to Dobërdol (1,800 m), a remote shepherd village inhabited only in summer. 16 to 17 km, 7 to 8 hours.
Day 5: a mountain pass on the Albania and Kosovo border, the climb to Gjeravica peak (2,656 m) and the descent to Gacafar (1,840 m), close to the Triple Border point. 16 to 17 km, 7 to 8 hours.
Day 6: the Triple Border Peak (2,366 m), a descent along the ridge between Kosovo and Montenegro, Lake Hrid, and the village of Babino Polje in Montenegro (1,550 m). 16 to 17 km, 7 to 8 hours.

Day 7: a short drive to the Grbaja valley, a climb through forest to Volušnica peak, and from there along a narrow ridge to Taljanka peak (2,056 m). Back down to the valley and a drive to the village of Vusanje (953 m). 20 to 22 km, 9 to 10 hours.

Day 8: a long day in the Prokletije reserve, crossing the border from Montenegro into Albania and descending to the village of Theth (750 m) for the last night in the mountains. 17 to 18 km, 7 to 8 hours.
Day 9: a short walk to the Grunas waterfall, a drive to the Blue Eye, a natural pool fed by a spring, and back to Shkodra. 6 to 7 km, 3 to 4 hours.
Day 10: transfer to Tirana airport and the flight home.

content.value: Full walking days last 7 to 8 hours in most cases. The longest is day 7: 20 to 22 km and 9 to 10 hours, with two summits and a descent of about 1,100 m. The biggest climb is on day 3, about 1,100 m from Valbona to the Prosllopi Pass. Days 2 and 9 are shorter and combine walking with driving.

content.title: ✦ High trail, low nights
content.value: The high point of the trek is Gjeravica peak, 2,656 m, but every night is spent at 1,840 m or lower. That is why altitude is not the main challenge here, and the itinerary has no acclimatization days. The challenge is the cumulative effort of eight walking days in a row.

content.value: Crossing a border on foot: the border permit

On most trips you cross a border once, at the airport. Here you cross on foot, several times, at mountain crossings with no border post and no passport control. To do this legally you need a border crossing permit, which is issued separately by the border police of each of the three countries, and each country has its own rules.

The application is submitted in advance, a few weeks before departure, with the passport details of every trekker and the date and place of every crossing. The permit covers the crossings and dates registered in it, so the route is planned ahead and not improvised on the ground. Anyone who crosses without a permit may be fined, which is why on every walking day your passport and the permits need to be with you, in your daypack.

content.title: ✦ Permits included
content.value: There is no passport control at the mountain crossings, but each crossing is approved in advance with the border police of each country. On our trek the border crossing permits between the countries are included in the price.
Because the application includes your passport details, it is worth checking your passport validity when you book, and not in the week before the flight.
Entering Albania, Kosovo and Montenegro

Citizens of the UK, the US, Canada, Australia and the EU do not need a visa for a tourist visit to any of the three countries (as of 2026). Travel with a valid passport, since the border permits are issued on your passport details, ideally valid for at least six months from the date you leave. Because the trek passes through three countries, it is important that you have no entry restriction for any of them. Entry rules can change, so check them for your nationality again before the flight.
Make sure your insurance policy covers mountain trekking in all three countries, including rescue, and check your government's current travel advice before you go.

One more practical detail: in Albania the currency is the lek, while Kosovo and Montenegro use the euro. In the mountain villages it is worth carrying cash for personal expenses, and tips for the guides are calculated in euros.
Guesthouses and food in the mountains

Throughout the trek you sleep in homely guesthouses in the mountain villages, run by local families. Rooms are shared, and during the trek there is no single room option. A single room is available only for the hotel nights in Shkodra, before and after the trek. The accommodation is simple, and that is part of the experience: anyone expecting hotel comfort will find something different here, and anyone looking for authenticity will find exactly that.

Three meals a day are included throughout the trek. Some are eaten at the guesthouses and some along the way: a traditional lunch at a restaurant on the boat day, lunch in the Buri meadow and coffee and mountain tea at a shepherd hut on day 3, and a picnic in a meadow of wildflowers on day 8. In Gacafar you are hosted by the Gacafari family, known for its warm hospitality and its mountain cooking.

Luggage is moved between the guesthouses, so on the trail you carry only a daypack. Some sections of the route have no mobile signal, so prepare your family in advance for quiet days. During the trek we send WhatsApp updates to families.
How hard is the trek, and who is it for

We grade the Peaks of the Balkans trek as moderate. There is no technical climbing, and it is a walking route from start to finish. The difficulty is cumulative: days of 13 to 22 km with ascents of up to about 1,100 m, day after day, and the ability to walk with a daypack for 7 to 9 hours. The descents are long too, and anyone with sensitive knees will feel them by the end of day 7. Trekking poles help on the climbs and descents.

No technical experience is required, and a previous multi-day trek is not a condition either. What matters is experience of long hikes in mountain terrain, because it teaches you how your body responds to a full day of climbs and descents. If you can walk about 20 km a day, enjoy a challenge and come with strong motivation, the trek can suit you. A medical certificate and a health declaration are required from every participant, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join.

Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call. The best preparation is long hikes with climbs and descents in the months before the trek, so that the second and third day in a row are not your first.

Good to know: the trek is led by professional local guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having. Every trekker must follow the instructions of the crew, and the route may change because of the weather or at the discretion of the guides. The group has satellite communication and an emergency evacuation plan, and in the mountains, as always, safety comes before reaching the goal.

content.value: When to go

The trekking season is summer and early fall, from June to October, and our groups depart in these months. Outside the season snow closes the high passes, and some of the villages along the way, such as Dobërdol, are inhabited only in summer.

At the start of the season, in June, patches of snow may still remain on the slopes and the high passes, and sometimes they last into July. At the end of the season, in October, the forests change color, and the first snow may already fall. Mountain weather changes quickly in every month, so even in summer bring a warm layer and a rain jacket. You will find the current dates on the trek page.
What it costs and what is included

The Peaks of the Balkans trek costs 1,750 euros per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Shkodra and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, 2 nights in a 3-star hotel in Shkodra with breakfast, accommodation in guesthouses and huts in shared rooms throughout the trek, three full meals a day throughout the trek, professional local English-speaking guides, luggage transfers between overnight stops throughout the trek, a boat ride on Lake Komani, all entry permits for the trek, live WhatsApp updates for families during the trek, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the trek, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap and a dry-fit shirt, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotel in Shkodra, personal gear (clothing and footwear), tips for the guides (50 euros per person), an extra hotel night if needed, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet. At extra cost you can add a single room at the hotel in Shkodra (40 euros a night).

If for any reason you need to leave the trek early, the guide accompanies you back safely and arranges what comes next. The additional costs that result, such as extra hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the traveler.
The Peaks of the Balkans with HighAir

At HighAir we take groups to the Peaks of the Balkans between June and October, in groups of up to 14 participants, to keep personal guidance and flexibility on the trail. The success rate we publish for this route is 96 percent.

Anyone who comes back from the Balkans wanting more can think about the next step: a longer trek, at high altitude. We also grade the Annapurna Circuit in Nepal as moderate, but it lasts 16 days and reaches a pass at 5,416 m, so acclimatization is a central part of that journey.

Frequently asked questions
How many days does the Peaks of the Balkans trek take?

The HighAir trek lasts 10 days, from landing in Tirana to the flight home. 8 of them are walking days in the mountains, with nights in guesthouses, plus two nights at a hotel in Shkodra, at the start and the end of the journey.
How hard is the Peaks of the Balkans trek?

We grade the trek as moderate. Full walking days range from 13 to 22 km, with ascents of up to about 1,100 m, and you need to be able to walk with a daypack for 7 to 9 hours. There is no technical climbing, but the effort is cumulative, so good fitness and experience of long hikes in mountain terrain matter.
Do you need a special permit to cross the borders on the trek?

Yes. The mountain crossings are not official border crossings, so you need a border crossing permit in advance from the border police of each of the three countries. On our trek the border crossing permits are included in the price. On walking days your passport needs to be with you.
Do I need a visa for Albania, Kosovo and Montenegro?

Citizens of the UK, the US, Canada, Australia and the EU enter all three countries for a tourist visit without a visa (as of 2026). Entry rules change, so check them for your nationality again before the flight and make sure you have no entry restriction for any of the countries.
Where do you sleep on the trek, and can you get a single room?

Throughout the trek you sleep in guesthouses run by local families, in shared rooms, with three meals a day. A single room is available only for the hotel nights in Shkodra, before and after the trek.
What language do the guides speak?
The trek is led by professional local English-speaking guides with long experience leading groups in the mountains.
